directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Yunnan camellia is less cold-hardy than Camellia japonica and best suited to zones 8-9. Prized among camellia specialists for producing some of the largest flowers of any camellia species, often eight inches or more across, with prominently veined, semi-double to fully double blooms in shades of rose-pink to deep red on a somewhat looser, more open-growing shrub than the denser, more familiar Camellia japonica. Native to the mountains of Yunnan province in southwestern China, it has been extensively hybridized with Camellia japonica to produce many of the largest-flowered modern camellia cultivars, though the pure species itself remains a coveted specimen for dedicated collectors. Provide the same acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and dappled shade other camellias require, protect from hard freezes given its somewhat reduced cold hardiness, and mulch well to keep roots cool and moist.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blood of China is an old, historic camellia cultivar valued for its dependable, vivid red winter bloom. One of the oldest camellia cultivars still commonly grown, dating to the early nineteenth century, it produces semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a vivid, saturated blood-red that opens over a long bloom season from fall through winter on a vigorous, upright shrub with glossy, deep green foliage. Its long history in Southern gardens and reliable, generous flowering have kept it in cultivation for two centuries, and it remains a benchmark red camellia against which newer introductions are still compared by collectors. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid overhead watering which can spot the flowers, and prune lightly after flowering finishes to shape if needed.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; High Hat camellia produces large, formal flowers on a compact, upright shrub. Large, formal double flowers open a clear, soft pink with neatly overlapping, evenly arranged petals in a classic, symmetrical form long favored by camellia show exhibitors, blooming over a long winter and early spring season on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub. Its reliable, high-quality flower form and manageable, upright habit have made it a long-standing favorite among camellia collectors and show growers seeking dependable, exhibition-quality blooms without a sprawling mature size. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid overhead watering which can spot the delicate petals, and prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Millie Mac azalea is a selection of the Gulf Coast native orange azalea with distinctive white-edged flowers. A striking selection of the native Florida flame azalea, it produces fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers in warm gold and orange tones distinctly edged in crisp white, a bicolor pattern not found in the straight species, opening in mid-spring on bare branches before or just as new leaves emerge and filling the garden with sweet fragrance. Like other native deciduous azaleas, it thrives in the dappled shade and acidic, humus-rich soil of a woodland edge, providing important early-season nectar for native bees and swallowtail butterflies migrating through the Gulf South. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, avoid heavy pruning since it flowers on the previous year's wood, and site in a location with good air movement to reduce fungal disease pressure.
